searchText: It depends on how you define it. I am working to make the spec as generic as possible, not tied to any specific algorithms or hardware. I.e., future-proof. It is challenging to have both performance and future-proofness. But not impossible! (I hope to have both.) For add/submod384, I want to keep the modular reduction as just a conditional subtraction/addition. This is the common case which we need to be fast. It would be nice to remove the "modulus must be odd" restriction. I have thought about this briefly, but I have not had time to focus on it yet. To clarify, add/submod384 don't have a "modulus must be odd" restriction. mulmodmont384 does. I would like to remove this restriction. There is one simple-and-dumb way to do that: count the number of 0 bits and represent m as `m * 2**e`, then use `x % m = (x - (x % 2**e)) % m + (x % 2**e) % m` Basically treat the higher bits and lower bits separately But I guess that could add bit twiddling overhead.... And counting 0 bits takes work, so this would work best with the "set modulus" method Or perhaps there's a generalization of montgomery that works well with gcd != 1? ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- So I want to have a more focused discussion on resurrection conflicts here at some point. It's a problem that I think it would be good to get us on the same page toward a solution for. See https://hackmd.io/@HWeNw8hNRimMm2m2GH56Cw/state_size_management#Resurrection-conflicts I think it's the key barrier toward implementing a "good" state expiry scheme And also my arguments for why we need storage-slot granularity a bit further above -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (Hah, I just read Koc's "Montgomery reduction with an even modulus" this morning which uses a trick like this to split the modulus just like you did.) Nice trick, glad you wrote it down. Yes, this may work with the "set modulus" method. Your suggestion is the best that I have seen. To be clear, I want `MULMODMONT` to compute the standard montgomery multiplication `(x*y*R^{-1}) % mod`. Not `(x*y) % mod`. right My math above was actually just doing `x % mod` I imagine that one day, there will be crypto coprocessors which can compute `x*y % mod` fast, but I assume they will go up to a certain bitwidth because of hardware size limitations. So `MULMODMONT` may still be needed for large bigints. But multiplying by invR during the reduction is a linear operation so it should still work If montgomery is faster in software might it not be faster in hardware as well? Good question. I don't know.
